senses: A light almond sponge cake.
ety: Thought to be named after the Mona Lisa (French La Joconde).
examples: The sponge itself is not the conventional Victoria but a thin and sumptuous joconde.
Flavours included a mandarin cake with a mandarin vanilla mousse and pineapple jam, and a pear cake with pear cardamom mousse with poached pear, pear jelly and almond joconde

senses: A transpersonal faculty of mind higher than the rational mind that might be translated as ‘intuitive intelligence’ or simply ‘higher mind’. It is ‘that which knows’, i.e. able to discern truth from falsehood.
The beneficiary of a warranty.
A style of black letter type, used especially in German-speaking countries from the 16th century until World War II.
A Pennsylvania German document style, incorporating watercolor illustration and fraktur lettering.
A bullpuppy, a bulldog puppy (of either sex).
ety: From bull + pup. The firearms sense originated from firearm designers in the United States during the 1930s. The unconventional configuration of bullpup rifles was compared by analogy to bulldog puppies, which were considered "squat, ugly, but still aggressive and powerful".

senses: Any seabird belonging to the genera Uria and Cepphus of the auk family Alcidae. They have black and white bodies and are good at swimming and diving.
That which limits or confines.
A friar who had a license to beg within certain bounds.
examples: The limiter automatically put on the brakes to keep the machine from going too fast.

senses: Dried salted cod; salt cod; klipfish.
ety: Borrowed from Portuguese bacalhau. Doublet of bacalao and baccala.

senses: Talk to little purpose; trifling talk; unmeaningful loquacity.
ety: From Middle English praten; either inherited from Old English prætt or borrowed via Middle Dutch or Middle Low German praten (from Old Saxon *pratt), all from Proto-West Germanic *prattu, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“idle or boastful talk, deceit”), from Proto-Indo-European *bred- (“to wander, rove”). Related to Dutch praten (“to talk, chat”), Low German praten, dated German pfrassen, Danish prate, Swedish prata (“to talk, prate”), Faroese práta (“to talk, gossip”), Icelandic prata;; also cognate with Polish bredzić (“to rave, jabber”), Latvian bradāt (“to talk nonsense”).

senses: Filtration through a semipermeable membrane that only allows small molecules through.

To intentionally lower or raise the pitch produced by a musical instrument, often to produce sounds not normally possible, or to reduce tension in a stringed instrument for the purpose of shipping or maintenance.
examples: Some avant-garde composers request that performers detune their instruments before playing.

senses: To heat food for the purpose of killing harmful organisms such as bacteria, viruses, protozoa, molds, and yeasts.
ety: Borrowed from French pasteuriser. From Louis Pasteur, the inventor of the process, + -ize.

senses: A night of (usually communal) Torah study.
One versed in acoustics, especially a physicist who specializes in acoustics.
Without a man or men.
Lacking masculinity.
ety: From Middle English manles, from Old English mannlēas, from Proto-Germanic *manalausaz, equivalent to man + -less. Cognate with Dutch manloos, German mannlos, Icelandic mannlauss.
examples: A eunuch is a negative creature. A beardless Moslem is contemptuously designated as manless.

senses: A feeling of dissatisfaction, anxiety, etc., caused by the dogged and ongoing pursuit of more goods and possessions.
A heavily modified or custom-built vehicle used in drag racing.
One who takes part in drag racing.
A workshop in an ancient Roman fort.
ety: Borrowed from Latin fabrica. Doublet of fabric and forge.

senses: A kind of freshwater catfish, the bronze corydoras (Corydoras aeneus).
ety: From the taxonomic name, from Latin aēneus (“bronze”).

senses: One who, or that which, judges.
A judgmental person (contrasted with perceiver as a personality type).
ety: From Middle English juger; equivalent to judge + -er.

senses: A place where meat, coffee, etc. is roasted.
ety: From roast + -ery. Doublet of rosticceria and rotisserie.
examples: Mr. Peet was born in 1920 in Alkmaar, the Netherlands, where he learned the coffee trade while cleaning machinery and running errands at his father’s small coffee roastery.

senses: A reddish variety of limestone.
ety: Borrowed from Italian scaglia (“a scale, a shell, a chip of marble”). Doublet of scale and shell.

senses: A crumbly topping for cakes and quick breads. It is made of sugar, flour, butter, and often other ingredients, especially cinnamon and chopped nuts.
ety: Borrowed from German Streusel. Related to strew.

senses: A deep-fried dumpling in American Asian cuisine, stuffed with a specified ingredient (typically crab).
examples: The box exploded on my chest, and I was covered from head to toe with chicken rangoon. I don't even like Chinese. No more Mr. Nice Guy. Ox launched himself at the fat man, hitting him square in his beer belly.

They ordered in Chinese—fried egg rolls, wontons stuffed with pork, crispy orange beef, greasy lo mein, and shrimp Rangoon. Fina ate until she was stuffed, took a long shower, and collapsed into Milloy's bed.

senses: The upper curvature of a horse's or dog's withers, back, and loin.
Top billing.
The first line, the topmost-ranking line; the most important thing.
The edge that runs along the top of the opening of a shoe.
The vocal parts of a piece of music (particularly pop).
examples: When viewing the horse in profile, attention must be paid to the curvature and proportions of the topline.
In recent weeks Cosby has, perhaps more than any other topline entertainer of the moment, been both at the pinnacle and at the crossroads.

senses: Having legs of a different tincture from that of the body.
A partial map that is automatically updated with new areas as the player discovers them.
The Germanic runic alphabet; especially specifically the Elder or Younger futhark alphabet (of Scandinavia and the European mainland), as contrasted with the Anglo-Saxon futhorc.
ety: From the first six letters of the runic alphabet, ᚠ (“f”), ᚢ (“u”), ᚦ (“þ”), ᚨ (“a”), ᚱ (“r”), ᚲ (“k”).

senses: Resembling or having properties of a membrane.
The removal of oxygen atoms or molecules from a material.
Agreement or concurrence for some end or purpose.
A plot between two or more people against somebody's wishes; conspiracy.
ety: From Middle English conspiracioun, from Middle French conspiration, from Latin cōnspīrātiō, cōnspīrātiōnem. Doublet of conspiracy.

senses: The smallest cutting from a root, stem, or leaf that can grow into a new plant.
A highly skilled and dedicated member of the police.
A jazz performer, especially one from the 1940s and 1950s.
A person associated with the jazz subculture of the 1940s and 1950s.
A sophisticated person, one who is stylish.
ety: From hep + cat, from hep (“sophisticated, aware”). Compare cat (“jazz enthusiast”). Attested in the sense of “sophisticated person” from the 1920s.

senses: Having, or formed as, a trellis.
examples: The station has only one platform, mostly of wooden construction, covered by a light trellised roof of timber and glass, with a single line on each side of it.

senses: A substance that has been adsorbed
A lancer, a soldier armed with a lance in a former light cavalry unit of the Polish, Prussian or German, Austrian, and Russian armies.
ety: From French uhlan, from German Uhlan, from Polish ułan, from Ottoman Turkish اوغلان (oğlan).

senses: The net-like construct of a spider containing sticky strands to catch prey.
Something that resembles a spider's web in being mesh-like, entrapping, or fragile.
ety: From Middle English spiþere webb, equivalent to spider + web.

senses: The role or status of chief.
An area or region governed by a chief.
A society larger than a tribe, but smaller or simpler than a state.
ety: From chief + -dom. Piecewise doublet of chefdom.

senses: A small piece of reflective glass or nacre that is hung indoors at a window to "catch the light".
